title: What a neural network actually computes
hook: No database, no rules: just weigh, add, bend. And why the kink, of all things, makes everything possible.

lines.text: When you talk to an AI, it's natural to assume there is a giant database of facts and rules inside.
In fact, there is nothing of the kind. Not a single stored sentence, not a single if-then rule.
A neural network is one single, very long formula. Numbers go in, numbers come out.
An image is just a list of brightness values. Text is turned into numbers first, too.
Inside the formula are adjustable dials, called weights. Large language models have hundreds of billions of them.
Everything the model can do lies in how those dials are set. Today, we look at what the formula actually computes.

</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<g ><line x1="298" y1="190" x2="338" y2="190" class="si"/><polygon points="348,190 338,195.5 338,184.5" class="fi"/></g>

<rect x="40" y="318" width="320" height="48" rx="12" class="fp"/>

</g>

lines.text: The building block is called a neuron. The name sounds like the brain, but the math behind it is school level.
A neuron receives several numbers as input. Each one is multiplied by its own weight.
The weight says how much that input matters. A negative weight means: this input counts against.
Then everything is added up, plus one extra number called the bias. It shifts the point at which the neuron switches on.
In the example: 0.5 times 2, plus minus 1 times 3, plus 1. That makes minus 1.

lines.text: How much brain is really in there? The idea dates from 1943, and even then it was a heavy simplification.
A real nerve cell fires short pulses, and their timing matters. The artificial neuron knows no time, only a single number.
Your brain has about 86 billion nerve cells with roughly 100 trillion connections. And it runs on about 20 watts.
Only one principle was borrowed: many simple units, connected with different strengths. Learning means changing those strengths.

scenes.title: The kink
scenes.svg:
<g data-l="0">
<g ><line x1="40" y1="240" x2="356" y2="240" class="sm"/><polygon points="366,240 356,245.5 356,234.5" class="fm"/></g>

<path d="M40 240 L200 240" class="fn sc s3" data-l="1" data-fx="draw"/>
<path d="M200 240 L330 110" class="fn sa s3" data-l="1" data-fx="draw" data-d="3.2"/>
<text x="112" y="214" class="mid ts fc" data-l="1" data-fx="up" data-d="2.2">below zero → 0</text>
<text x="322" y="170" class="mid ts fa" data-l="1" data-fx="up" data-d="5">stays</text>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="pop" data-d="2.5"><circle cx="140" cy="240" r="8" class="fb"/></g>
<text x="140" y="268" class="mid tm fb tb" data-l="2" data-fx="up" data-d="2.5">−1 → 0</text>
<path d="M40 237 C140 236 176 232 200 220 S 280 150 328 100" class="fn se dash" data-l="3"/>
<text x="268" y="120" class="end ts fe" data-l="3" data-fx="up">soft kink</text>
<g data-l="4"><circle cx="200" cy="240" r="17" class="fn sb pulse"/></g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="64" y="298" width="272" height="44" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="326" class="mid tm">Without the kink: worthless</text>
</g>

lines.text: Now comes the step that everything depends on. The result is passed through a so-called activation function.
The most popular one is called ReLU, and it is surprisingly simple: anything below zero becomes zero. Anything above stays as it is.
Drawn as a curve, that is a straight line with a kink. Our minus one from before becomes zero. The neuron stays silent.
There are versions with a softer kink. The idea stays the same.
The kink looks unremarkable. But without it, the whole network would be worthless. That is the first point that is not obvious.

lines.text: Imagine a network without the kink. Each layer only multiplies and adds.
But multiplying and adding, done several times in a row, is still just multiplying and adding.
So a hundred such layers can be merged into a single one. Mathematically, the result is exactly the same.
A network like that could only model straight-line relationships: double the input, double the effect.
But the world is not a straight line. The kink is what makes depth useful, because each layer can do something the previous one could not.

lines.text: What does this mean geometrically? Take two inputs and plot them as a point on a surface.
A neuron draws a straight boundary across that surface. The weights set its direction, the bias sets its position.
On one side, the neuron stays silent. On the other, it gets louder the farther the point lies from the boundary.
So a neuron is a detector for one single direction in space. Nothing more.
A layer is many neurons side by side. They all see the same inputs, but each one looks in a different direction.

<text x="200" y="346" class="mid tm" data-l="2" data-fx="up">1969: proven impossible for one neuron</text>
<text x="200" y="376" class="mid tm fd tb" data-l="3" data-fx="up" data-d="3.5">Solution: one layer before it</text>

lines.text: And this is where it gets interesting. Look at these four points: two blue, two yellow, arranged crosswise.
Try to separate them with one single straight line. It cannot be done, however you turn it.
In the late 1960s, it was proven that a single neuron cannot solve this problem.
That is one reason why enthusiasm for neural networks collapsed for many years. Yet the solution was just one layer away.

lines.text: The solution is one more layer in front, and you can picture it with a sheet of paper.
Fold the sheet along the diagonal through the two blue points. The yellow points now lie exactly on top of each other.
In the folded sheet, one straight boundary is enough: close to the fold is blue, farther away is yellow.
That is exactly what two neurons with a kink do. Each measures the distance from the diagonal, one on each side.
This is the basic principle of every neural network: bend the space, layer by layer, until the problem becomes easy.
This idea generalizes. Every neuron contributes one kink.
With two kinks, you hit a curve only roughly. With eight, quite well. With a thousand, you can no longer see a difference.
It is mathematically proven: with enough neurons, you can rebuild practically any relationship without jumps, as precisely as you like.
The catch: the proof only says that suitable weights exist. It does not say how to find them.
Finding them is the real trick. It is called training, and that is the topic of the next AI episode.

scenes.title: Depth beats width

lines.text: Why are networks built deep, with many layers in a row, instead of one single huge layer?
Think of the paper again. One fold gives two layers, two folds give four. After ten folds, there are more than a thousand.
Each layer folds what the earlier ones already folded. With depth, expressive power can multiply. With width, it only grows slowly.
That is why the field is called deep learning. Depth is not a buzzword. It is the trick for building very complex shapes from few parts.

lines.text: What forms inside the layers can be made visible. In networks that recognize images, the same pattern shows up again and again.
The early layers respond to edges and color changes. The middle ones respond to textures and parts, such as an eye or a wheel.
The late layers respond to whole objects. Nobody programmed that. This hierarchy emerges by itself during training.
This may be the most astonishing part: we only build the empty formula. What each dial means, the network works out on its own.

lines.text: And what does this have to do with language? More than you might think.
A word is also first turned into a list of numbers, so it becomes a point. Only this point lies in a space with thousands of directions instead of two.
The layers bend this space until things with similar meaning end up close together.
At its core, a language model does the same as our mini network. Just with hundreds of billions of weights instead of nine.
There are some extra parts, above all the so-called attention. But the basic computation stays: weigh, add, bend.

lines.text: What comes out of a language model at the end? Not a finished sentence, but once again a list of numbers.
For every possible next word, it holds a probability. After “The sky is”, for example: “blue” very high, “green” very low.
One word is drawn from this list and appended. Then the whole formula runs again, for the next word.
So a long text is built word by word, through thousands of runs of the same formula. How that works in detail gets its own episode.

lines.text: Three things follow from this. They explain why AI behaves the way it does.
First: knowledge does not sit in one place. It is smeared across millions of weights. That is why you cannot simply delete a mistake like a row in a database.
Second: the network looks nothing up, it computes. Even where it has never seen examples, it just keeps computing. That is the root of hallucinations.
Third: the same property is its strength. Because similar things lie close together, it can handle cases it has never seen.
Remember three words: weigh, add, bend. In the next AI episode, we look at how a network finds its weights by itself.

takeaways: A neural network is one long formula with adjustable numbers (weights). It contains no rules and no stored sentences.
A neuron computes: inputs times weights, add everything up, add the bias, then pass it through the kink (ReLU: below zero becomes zero).
Without the kink, any number of layers could be merged into a single one. The kink is what makes depth useful.
Geometrically, each neuron draws a boundary. Layers fold the space until a hard problem can be solved with one straight boundary.
Enough neurons can rebuild almost any relationship. Finding the right weights is the real difficulty (training).
Knowledge is spread across the weights. That explains why mistakes are hard to delete, why models hallucinate, and why they can generalize.
